fact_en: Thick fog makes it hard to see distant things, so drivers must slow down and be extra careful!
fact_bis: Sa baga nga gabon, lisod makita ang halayo nga mga butang, mao nga angay mag-amping ang mga drayber!

findings.note: title_en "Thick Fog on Roads" → title_bis "Yabo sa Dalan" = "a spill on the road" — which in a road-safety card reads as a real and different hazard (spilled liquid), not fog. Body is correct Cebuano ("Sa baga nga gabon, lisod makita ang halayo nga mga butang"), so the title alone carries the wrong thing; of the three yabo cards in this batch this is the one where the wrong word is independently plausible and therefore most likely to be believed.

fact_en: Dew is the tiny drops of water you see sparkling on grass and leaves in the early morning!
fact_bis: Ang yamog mao ang gagmayng tinulo sa tubig nga makita sa sagbot ug mga dahon kada buntag!

findings.note: title_en "Morning Dew" but title_bis = "Gabon sa Buntag" — gabon is FOG, not dew. The card's own body uses the right word ("Ang yamog mao ang gagmayng tinulo sa tubig nga makita sa sagbot ug mga dahon kada buntag"), so the title is the outlier, and the sibling card in this same batch (ffct-30361) exists specifically to teach that fog and dew are NOT the same ("ang gabon maporma sa hangin mismo, samtang ang yamog maporma sa ibabaw sa mga butang"). A Cebuano-only child reading the heading is taught the exact conflation the neighbouring card corrects. Corpus cross-check: every other dew title uses yamog/hamog (Yamog sa Dahon, Hamog sa Gabii, Punto sa Hamog); this is the only gabon-titled dew card.

fact_en: In places like Manila, the land is also sinking, so the sea seems to rise even faster!
fact_bis: Sa pipila ka lugar sama sa Manila, naglubog usab ang yuta, busa morag mas paspas mosaka ang dagat!

findings.note: "Sinking Land in Manila" -> title_bis "Nalubog nga Yuta sa Manila" and body "naglubog usab ang yuta". Tagalog lubog = submerged/sinking, but Cebuano lubog = murky/turbid (lubog nga tubig); to sink is lunod/unlod. The card's whole fact is that Manila's land is subsiding, and nothing in the card restores it — read as Cebuano the sentence becomes "the land is also getting murky, so the sea seems to rise faster", which does not deliver subsidence. Corpus-internal evidence that lubog is the outlier: sibling cards use the correct word for submersion (ffct-30542 "mahimong malunod", ffct-30543 "kung malunod ang baybayon").

fact_en: Clouds come in fun shapes! Cumulus look like fluffy cotton balls, stratus form flat layers, and cirrus are high and wispy.
fact_bis: Nagkalainlain ang porma sa panganod! Ang cumulus murag humok nga bulak, ang stratus patag nga sapaw, ug ang cirrus taas ug mahimulmol.

findings.note: EN "Cumulus look like fluffy cotton balls" -> "Ang cumulus murag humok nga bulak". Tagalog bulak = cotton, but Cebuano bulak = FLOWER (cotton in Cebuano is gapas). The card never corrects it, so a Cebuano-only reader is told cumulus clouds look like soft flowers rather than cotton balls — a different object, and the comparison is the only content the card gives for cumulus. Honest caveat: "humok" still conveys softness, so the fluffiness survives even though the named object does not.

fact_en:
What scale do scientists use for really big earthquakes today?

For huge earthquakes, scientists now use the moment magnitude scale (Mw) — it's more accurate than the old Richter scale!
fact_bis:
Unhang scale ang gigamit sa mga siyentista karon para sa daghan kaayong mga linog?

Para sa daghang mga linog, ang mga siyentista karon naggamit sa moment magnitude scale (Mw) — mas tukma kini kay sa daan nga Richter scale!

findings.note: EN "What scale do scientists use for really big earthquakes today? ... For huge earthquakes, scientists now use the moment magnitude scale (Mw)" becomes "para sa daghan kaayong mga linog" / "Para sa daghang mga linog" = "for VERY MANY earthquakes". Size is swapped for quantity in BOTH the question and the answer, and title_bis ("Moment sa Magnitude") does not restore it: the card never says dako/kusog anywhere. A Cebuano-only reader learns that Mw is the scale used when there are many earthquakes, which is false and leaves the real fact (Mw is for the largest quakes) unrecoverable. Cebuano daghan = many/numerous; big = dako.

fact_en: The Moon's pull causes ocean tides to rise and fall, and they are strongest at new and full moons!
fact_bis: Ang birik sa Bulan maoy hinungdan sa pagtaob ug paghunas sa dagat, ug mas kusog ang taob panahon sa bag-ong bulan o takdol!

findings.note: EN "The Moon's pull causes ocean tides to rise and fall" -> BIS "Ang birik sa Bulan maoy hinungdan sa pagtaob ug paghunas sa dagat". In Cebuano 'birik' is to spin/rotate (bira/guyod/hila = pull; gravity = grabidad), so a Cebuano-only child is taught that the Moon's SPIN drives the tides - a different mechanism from gravitational pull, and the misconception the card exists to prevent. Nothing in the card corrects it: the title is just "Bulan ug Tides" and 'birik' is the emph_bis highlight, so it is the word the UI pushes at the child. The corpus's own sibling card on the same fact says it correctly - ffct-02394: "Ang gravity sa Bulan mao ang nag-unang hinungdan sa tides" - which is what makes this card the outlier. Confidence low-to-medium: 'birik' appears only 3x in the whole corpus and all 3 render English "pull" (ffct-16313 "birik sa grabidad", ffct-32028 "birik sa Adlaw"), so this looks like one translator's systematic (and I believe wrong) choice rather than a one-off slip; if a native speaker accepts 'birik' for gravitational attraction, all three cards pass together.

fact_en: Fog is like a cloud sitting right on the ground! It's made of tiny water droplets floating in the air, making it hard to see — just like in Baguio or the mountains!
fact_bis: Ang gabon morag panganod nga naglingkod sa yuta! Hinimo kini sa gagmay nga tulo sa tubig nga naglutaw, mao nga malabo ang tan-aw — sama sa Baguio o sa kabukiran!

findings.note: title_bis "Yabo nga Panganod sa Yuta" for "Fog, a Ground Cloud": Cebuano *yabo* means to spill/pour out (corpus uses it that way in ffct-15651 "sa pagyabo", ffct-08616 "pag-yabo sa tubig", ffct-25761 "dili mayabo ang tubig"), not fog. The card's OWN body uses the correct word — "Ang gabon morag panganod nga naglingkod sa yuta" — so the title is the outlier. Systematic: 234.json ffct-34846 titles "Fog in Baguio" as "Yabo sa Baguio" too. A child reading the title learns fog = yabo, which is false vocabulary for the card's own subject.

fact_en: Clouds float and move across the sky because the wind carries them! That's why their shapes and positions keep changing all the time.
fact_bis: Nagalupad ug naglihok ang mga panganod kay gidala sa hangin! Mao nga kanunay nga mausab ang ilang porma ug posisyon.

findings.note: title_bis "Liwat sa mga Panganod" for "Clouds Move with Wind": Cebuano *liwat* means to resemble / take after (kaliwat = breed, lineage, descendants — see ffct-04650, ffct-03948, ffct-13087 in this corpus), not movement, which is *lihok*. The card's own body uses the right word ("Nagalupad ug naglihok ang mga panganod kay gidala sa hangin"), so the title names a different thing than the English. Systematic across titles: ffct-24165 "Inertia sa Pundo ug Liwat" (Motion), ffct-12559 "Adlaw-adlaw nga Liwat sa Bata" (Daily Activity), ffct-11361 "Kusang ug Tuyo nga Liwat" (Moves) — all with bodies that correctly say lihok.

fact_en:
Why are lower signals warned earlier?

Lower signals are warned earlier because strong winds are still far away, while higher signals mean they are coming very soon!
fact_bis:
Nganong mas sayo ang pasidaan sa mas ubos nga signal?

Mas sayo ang pasidaan sa mas ubos nga signal kay layo pa ang kusog nga hangin, samtang sa taas nga signal, hapit na kini!

findings.note: title_bis "Babag sa Ubos nga Signal" uses babag = OBSTACLE/blockage where English is "warning" (Early Low-Signal Warnings). Title reads "Obstruction at the low signal" — names a different thing and also drops the "early/lead time" point that is the whole card. Body uses the correct word pasidaan throughout, so the title is the outlier.

fact_en:
What fuel does the Sun use to keep shining?

Hydrogen! The Sun shines by using its hydrogen like fuel through fusion in its core.
fact_bis:
Unong 'sugnod' ang gigamit sa Adlaw aron mosidlak?

Hydrogen! Nagsidlak ang Adlaw pinaagi sa paggamit sa hydrogen niini nga morag sugnod pinaagi sa fusion sa ubod.

findings.note: title_bis "Hydrogen nga Sobra sa Adlaw" = "excess/left-over hydrogen in the Sun", but the card is "Hydrogen Fuels the Sun". Sobra (excess) is not fuel; a child reading the title is told the Sun has surplus hydrogen rather than that hydrogen is its fuel. Body uses the correct word sugnod (and terms list sugnod/gatong), so the title is the outlier.

fact_en:
Why do we call oil, gas, and coal fossil fuels?

They are called fossil fuels because they come from ancient plants and animals that died millions of years ago!
fact_bis:
Nganong gitawag og fossil fuels ang langis, gas, ug karbon?

Gitawag sila og fossil fuels kay naggikan kini sa mga tanom ug hayop nga namatay milyon ka tuig na ang milabay!

findings.note: title_bis "Karaang Kinabuhi Fue" ends in the non-word "Fue" — a truncated "Fuel"/"Fuels". The title therefore never says what the card is about (fossil fuels); it reads "Ancient Life Fue". Not register or compact style — the word is cut off. Body is correct ("fossil fuels ang langis, gas, ug karbon").

fact_en:
Could a black hole swallow Earth?

No need to fear! The nearest known black holes are thousands of light-years away—way too far to pull Earth toward them.
fact_bis:
Mahimo bang tukbon sa Yuta ang black hole?

Dili angay mahadlok! Ang pinakaduol nga black hole libo-libong light-years ang layo—layo kaayo nga makabira sa Yuta.

findings.note: Direction reversal in the question, plus a dropped negation in the answer. EN: "Could a black hole swallow Earth?" BIS: "Mahimo bang TUKBON SA YUTA ang black hole?" — in Cebuano patient-focus, the sa-phrase is the agent and the ang-phrase the patient, so this asks "Can the EARTH swallow the BLACK HOLE?", the exact opposite. Correct would be "Matukob/Mahurot ba sa black hole ang Yuta?". The answer does not repair it and adds a second problem: "layo kaayo NGA makabira sa Yuta" uses the Cebuano "X kaayo nga Y" result construction, so it reads "so far away THAT IT CAN pull the Earth" — the English "too far TO pull Earth" needs a negative/purpose form (e.g. "layo ra kaayo para makabira sa Yuta" or "dili na makabira sa Yuta"). A Cebuano-only child gets a reversed question and an answer that literally affirms the black hole can pull Earth.
